# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-2 (Extended v27)

## Setting and Time
- Multiple time periods: French Revolution era; Napoleonic coronation epoch; 1809 (Pope's arrest); 1811 (Bishop's synod attendance); 1813 onward (Napoleon's decline); **1815 (Bishop's 75th birthday, early October—evening/night of Valjean's theft and flight); 1817 (carrier sighting; young Parisians' Saint-Cloud excursion and Bombarda's restaurant dinner); 1818 spring (Montfermeil cook-shop with Thénardier family and Fantine's arrival); 1862 (narrative reflection on changed Paris)**; present day (spring transitioning to late August/early September, England); future wedding (following spring); 1795 (Jean Valjean's theft at Faverolles and trial)
- Primary locations: England (Hampstead, Hull, Liverpool, Dunstead/Kelford harbor towns, Suffolk, London, Welbeck Street, Lowestoft, Torton, Kelmere, Dunby, Yarlby); Secondary locations: San Francisco, New York, Eastern Prussia, Germany, Hamburgh; French locations (D——, Manosque, Sisteron, Hautes-Alpes, Paris, Italy, Durance, Château-Arnoux, Senez, Briançon, Aix, Draguignan, Embrun, Chastelar, Arche, Barcelonette, Jauziers, Tuiles, Joug-de-l'Aigle, Ubaye, Ubayette, Ollioules, Nice, Piédmont, Couloubrieux, Cannes, Rue Cassette, Elmhaven, Staveford, Grenoble, Bras d'Asse, Escoublon, Grasse, Franche-Comté, Pontarlier, Lods, Châtillon, Audincourt, Beure, Faverolles, Brie, Tottlingen, Toulon, Quenford, Ravenmere, Basses-Alpes, Latin Quarter Paris, Mount Sainte-Geneviève, Toulouse, Cahors, Limoges, Montauban, Naples, Saint-Cloud, Fécamp, Vanvres, Issy, Passy, l'Étoile, Champs-Élysées, Rue de Rivoli, Delorme Alley, Place de la Concorde, Place Louis XV, Avenue de Neuilly, Tuileries, Marigny square, Odéon, Luxembourg, Rue Madame, Allée de l'Observatoire, Saint-Jacques-du-Haut-Pas, Coural das Freiras vineyard, Madeira, Montfermeil, Boulanger Lane, Villemomble, Salcombe, Gulhaven, M. sur M.)
- **October 1815 evening in D——**: Sunset approaching; frost silvered hedges; rain threatening; salt and tar smell on wind; bell for vespers; baker's boy late; children with hoop; cart with turnips; gulls over fish heads. Supper at eight o'clock with Bishop, Baptistine, Madame Magloire. **Night after supper: Valjean's theft and flight post-midnight. Following morning (October 1815): Bishop at breakfast remarks contentedly about bread and milk.**
- **1818 spring at Montfermeil, Boulanger Lane (recurring atmospheric descriptions)**: Evening at cook-shop kept by Thénardier family. Recurring imagery: bell for vespers rings thinly; children chase hoop shrieking; bees hum in lavender behind parsonage; chalked crooked sun on forge wall; cart with turnips creaks past well; gulls quarrel over fish heads; dog barks then goes quiet; frost silvered hedges overnight; light went early; road rutted and puddled after thaw; wind off water with salt and tar smell; smoke from chimneys lay flat over fields; baker's boy late, line at oven grew long.
- **Fantine's arrival at Montfermeil (1818 spring, middle of day)**: After traveling several leagues via suburban coach service from Paris (set out on foot carrying child, took Villemomble coach when met it, walked remainder). Child (Cosette) walked little; Fantine obliged to carry her.

## Main Characters and Relationships

**M. Charles Myriel / Monseigneur Bienvenu (Bishop)**
- French aristocrat; family ruined by Revolution; emigrated to Italy; wife died
- Became priest, then Bishop of D——; encountered Napoleon circa coronation epoch
- Redistributes entire 15,000 franc yearly State salary across 23 charitable categories; retains 1,500 francs yearly for personal sustenance
- Philosophy: society culpable for poverty and ignorance; strives to dress wounds and relieve suffering
- Attended condemned murderer's execution; experienced deep moral crisis regarding scaffold
- **Bandit incident**: After destruction of Gaspard Bès's band, lieutenant Cravatte deposited chest with stolen pontifical vestments from Notre Dame d'Embrun with paper reading: "From Cravatte to Monseigneur Bienvenu"
- 1809: Summoned by Napoleon to synod; 1811 (June 15): Attended synod at Notre-Dame
- Political views: From 1813, gave adherence to hostile manifestations against Napoleon; refused to see him returning from Elba; acknowledged his own hour of party spirit and bitterness; was Royalist
- **1815 (October evening)**: Aged 75, appeared no more than 60; rather plump; long strides on foot; step firm. Warmly accepts Valjean at supper; explains fruitières of Pontarlier. After supper: Mother Gerbaud visits with child; Bishop kisses child, borrows fifteen sous to give her. Tells Valjean: "You must be in great need of your bed." Says grace, instructs table clearing. Sends goat skin from Black Forest to Valjean's bed for warmth. Knelt before altar, said brief prayer. Made strange abrupt movement—folded arms, bent savage gaze upon guest, exclaimed in hoarse voice (words unspecified)—moment unclear in intent
- **At parting (moment unspecified but before theft)**: Told Valjean: "You have promised me to become an honest man. I buy your soul. I take it away from the spirit of perversity; I give it to the good God"
- **Following morning (October 1815)**: Bent examining plant of cochlearia broken by fallen silver basket; rose at Madame Magloire's cry. At breakfast remarked gayly one does not need fork or spoon to dip bread in milk

**Mademoiselle Baptistine** (Bishop's sister)
- Long, pale, thin, gentle creature; embodiment of respectability; acquired beauty of goodness
- Yearly income 500 francs
- Possesses goat skin from Black Forest and little ivory-handled knife
- **October 1815 evening**: At supper with Valjean; peaceable and natural. Following morning: said nothing at breakfast

**Madame Magloire** (Bishop's servant)
- Only servant; eventually accustomed to Bishop's openness
- **October 1815 evening**: Warned about prowler—dangerous mendicant in town; Labarre refused him; vagabond roamed streets at gloaming via boulevard Gassendi. Proposed locksmith Paulin Musebois replace ancient locks. At supper, placed three sets of forks and spoons; when Bishop had guest, laid out all six silver sets on tablecloth—innocent ostentation. After supper, cleared table very promptly. Carried goat skin to Valjean's bed. Placed six silver sets in little cupboard near head of bed on right side entering from dining-room
- **Night of theft**: With alertness of old woman, rushed to oratory, returned to report discovery
- **Following morning**: Grumbled under breath at breakfast

**Jean Valjean**
- **Background**: Born poor peasant family of Brie; did not learn to read in childhood. Became tree-pruner at Faverolles. Mother Jeanne Mathieu; father Jean Valjean (sobriquet). Lost both parents early; sister older, widow with seven children, raised him
- **At approximately 25-26 years (1795)**: Took father's place, supported sister; spent youth in rude, ill-paid toil
- **1795 theft and trial**: Sunday evening, Maubert Isabeau (baker on Church Square, Faverolles) caught Valjean stealing loaf; arm bled through grated hole. Taken before tribunals for theft and breaking and entering inhabited house at night. Had gun (better poacher than marksman, injured case). Condemned to five years galleys; set out for Toulon after 27-day journey
- **Toulon imprisonment (19 years total)**: Clothed in red cassock; effaced identity; became number 24,601. Reflected society culpable for poverty; recognized chastisement ferocious and disproportioned. Four escape attempts, aggravations complicated sentence. Worth four men at work; nicknamed "Jean the Jack-screw." Possessed climbing ability. Spoke little, laughed not. At age 40 learned to read, write, cipher; intelligence fortified hate. Sentence extended to nineteen years total
- **Liberation (unspecified date)**: Upon hearing "Thou art free!" moment seemed improbable. Yellow passport provided. Calculated earnings 171 francs, reduced to 109 francs fifteen sous; felt wronged and robbed
- **Post-liberation labor (Grasse, before D——)**: Unloaded bales at orange-flower distillery; worked intelligently. Master pleased. Gendarme demanded papers; showed yellow passport. Evening, master paid fifteen sous. Valjean objected. Told "That is enough for thee." Master warned: "Beware of the prison"
- **Appearance on arrival at D——, October 1815**: Medium stature, thickset, robust, approximately 46 years old. Cap with drooping leather visor; face burned, tanned, perspiring. Coarse yellow linen shirt with silver anchor. Twisted string cravat; worn threadbare blue drilling trousers. Old gray tattered blouse patched with green cloth. Packed knapsack. Enormous knotty stick. Iron-shod shoes on stockingless feet. Shaved head and long beard. Thoughtful but not gloomy; peculiar affectionate nature; something decidedly sluggish and insignificant about appearance
- **October 1815 evening supper**: Stated: "I am a galley-slave; a convict" and unfolded yellow passport. Overwhelmed by acceptance, exclaimed about not being driven forth, being called "sir," bed with sheets. Had spent only twenty-five sous in four days
- **Theft and subsequent spiritual crisis**: Seized silver, fled. Post-theft (October 1815 afternoon-evening, three leagues from D——): Sat on deserted plain. Encountered Little Gervais, robbed forty sous. Searched unsuccessfully for child. Psychological crisis: Bishop's pardon eclipsed Valjean's self-image; wept at intersection of three paths. **Mystical vision**: Conscience weighed Bishop and Jean Valjean; Bishop grew resplendent while Valjean vanished; only Bishop remained, filled whole soul with magnificent radiance. Wept as past life recurred with unprecedented clarity; examined life and soul; seemed horrible and frightful. Gentle light rested over life and soul; perceived Satan by light of Paradise. **Crisis marked decisive transformation through divine confrontation with virtue's radiance.**

**Fantine (the Blonde)**
- **1817 status**: Beautiful, sunny hair; youngest grisette; still in first illusions; radiant, perfumed; retained serenity of toil and flower of honesty. Brilliant of face, delicate profile, deep blue eyes, heavy lids, small arched feet, admirably formed wrists and ankles, white skin showing azure vein branching, young fresh cheek, robust throat, strong supple nape, shoulders modelled (Coustou-like), voluptuous dimple visible through muslin. Gayety cooled by dreaminess; sculptural and exquisite. Rare dreamer whose face revealed ancient sacred euphony; thoroughbred; beautiful in style and rhythm. In love. Hedged about with vague resistance composed of dreaminess and wildness; "always have queer look about you" (per Favourite)
- **Mistress of Félix Tholomyès (1817)**; dazzled by simplest things. **Decision by Tholomyès (1817): Abandoned by Tholomyès; he departs to return to parents via Toulouse diligence**
- **1818 spring (Montfermeil)**: Transformed, difficult to recognize. Young, but appearance sad and poverty-stricken; dressed like working-woman inclined to turn peasant. Golden lock of thick hair escaped but severely concealed beneath ugly, tight, nun-like cap tied under chin. Did not smile. Eyes had not been dry for very long. Pale; weary and rather sickly appearance. Gazed upon sleeping daughter with air peculiar to nursing mother. Large blue handkerchief (like Invalides use) folded into fichu concealing figure clumsily. Hands sunburnt and dotted with freckles; forefinger hardened and lacerated with needle. Wore cloak of coarse brown woollen stuff, linen gown, coarse shoes. **Aerial toilette of muslin and ribbons—made of mirth, folly, music, bells, perfumed with lilacs—had vanished like hoar-frost mistaken for diamonds; melts leaving branch black.**
- **1818 spring proposal to Madame Thénardier at Montfermeil**: Cannot take daughter to country; work will not permit it; with child one can find no situation. Paid initial fee (50-57 francs per narrative); passed night at inn, gave up money, left child, fastened carpet-bag, set out following morning intending to return soon. **Claim**: People arrange such departures tranquilly; but they are despairs. Expected return not materially delayed
- **Payment arrangement (1818 onward)**: First six months after mother departed: mother sent seven francs per month with tolerable regularity. After sixth month completed, Thénardier demanded increase to twelve francs monthly (persuaded mother child was happy and coming on well); mother submitted and forwarded twelve francs. Subsequently Thénardier, learning child probably bastard and mother could not acknowledge it, exacted fifteen francs per month, claiming child was growing, eating, and threatening to send her away. Mother (now at M. sur M.) became irregular in payments; some months in arrears

**Cosette (Euphrasie)**
- **Full name**: Euphrasie; mother calls her Cosette (diminutive via mothers' and populace's sweet instinct, like Josepha→Pepita, Françoise→Sillette; etymologists mystified; grandmother once transformed Theodore into Gnon)
- **Age (1818 spring)**: Two or three years old
- **Appearance at arrival (1818 spring)**: Most divine creature; coquettish dress with fine linen cap, ribbons on bodice, Valenciennes lace on cap. Skirt folds raised showing white, firm, dimpled leg. Admirably rosy and healthy; inspired desire to bite apples of cheeks. Great blue eyes like mother's with magnificent lashes. Serious and sometimes severe air of little children—mystery of luminous innocence in presence of twilight of virtue; seemed angels knowing us men
- **Behavior at Montfermeil arrival (1818 spring)**: Awakened by mother's passionate kiss; opened blue eyes; looked at nothing with child's seriousness. Began to laugh; slipped to ground with unconquerable energy wishing to run; caught sight of two Thénardier daughters in swing, stopped short, put out tongue in sign of admiration. Asleep when mother initially arrived at inn
- **Subsequent treatment by Thénardiers (post-1818 spring)**: After mother's money spent and outfit pawned for sixty francs, Thénardiers treated her merely as charity case. Dressed in cast-off petticoats and chemises of Thénardier daughters; that is, rags. Fed on what rest had left—little better than dog, little worse than cat. Cat and dog were habitual table-companions; Cosette ate with them under table from wooden bowl similar to theirs. Made to run on errands, sweep rooms/courtyard/street, wash dishes, carry burdens. Called the _Lark_ in neighborhood. Populace bestowed this name on trembling, frightened, shivering little creature, no bigger than bird, awake every morning before anyone else in house or village, always in street or fields before daybreak
- **Treatment by Madame Thénardier**: Woman possessed load of caresses and burden of blows and injuries to dispense each day. If not for Cosette, daughters would have received whole amount; but stranger diverted blows to herself. Daughters received nothing but caresses. Cosette could not make motion without drawing heavy shower of violent blows and unmerited chastisement. Sweet, feeble being, who should not have understood anything of world or God, incessantly punished, scolded, ill-used, beaten, seeing beside her two little creatures like herself, who lived in ray of dawn

**Thénardier Family**
- **Thénardier and wife**: Keep cook-shop at Montfermeil on Boulanger Lane, circa 1818 spring; establishment still exists by narrative time (unspecified later reference). **Sign: painted man carrying another man with gilt epaulettes of general, silver stars, red spots representing blood, smoke representing battle. Inscription: "AT THE SIGN OF SERGEANT OF WATERLOO"**
- **Thénardier character**: Troublesome for physiognomist. One can only look at some men to distrust them; dark in both directions. Uneasy in rear and threatening in front. Shadow in glance denounces them. From merely hearing them utter word or seeing them make gesture, glimpse sombre secrets in past and sombre mysteries in future. Claims to have been soldier—sergeant; probably conducted himself with tolerable valor in campaign of 1815 (truth content uncertain). Painted hostelry sign himself; knew how to do little of everything, and badly. Dwarfed nature susceptible to hideous progress toward evil; material for blackguard. Possessed crab-like soul continually retreating toward darkness, retrograding rather than advancing, employing experience to augment deformity, growing incessantly worse, becoming more impregnated with ever-augmenting blackness
- **Madame Thénardier**: Sandy-complexioned, thin and angular—type of soldier's wife in all its unpleasantness; languishing air from reading romances. Simpering but masculine creature. Still young; barely thirty. When crouching, not apparent; if stood upright, lofty stature and frame of perambulating colossus suitable for fairs might have frightened traveller outset, troubled confidence. **Critical fact**: Person seated instead of standing erect—destinies hang upon such thing. Dwarfed nature susceptible to hideous progress toward evil; brute substratum; possessed crab-like soul. Possessed load of caresses and burden of blows and injuries to dispense each day
- **Two unnamed daughters**: Approximately two and a half years old and eighteen months old (1818 spring); seated together in chain loop under fore-carriage of timber truck outside cook-shop, held by knotted handkerchief. Happy, pretty, clean. Mother allowed them to use chain as plaything. Idolized by mother; received all caresses while Cosette received blows
- **Financial situation**: Thanks to Fantine's initial 50-57 francs, Thénardier able to avoid protest and honor signature. Following month again in need of money

## Secondary and Supporting Characters
- **Young Parisians (Four Oscars) of 1817**: Félix Tholomyès (Toulouse, 30, 4,000 francs yearly; badly preserved; bald, toothless, wrinkled; mediocre digestion; weeping eye; ironic philosopher; advocates meditation in dining; disparages excess zeal; abandoned Fantine); Listolier (Cahors); Fameuil (Limoges); Blachevelle (Montauban, very stingy, departed 1817)
- **Four grisettes**: Dahlia (more experienced, heedless, emancipated); Zéphine (more experienced, heedless, emancipated); Favourite (been to England; father mathematics professor brutal braggart; mother devotee air, cross, pious, silent; adores/detests Blachevelle; admires young actor opposite house; spleen, butter prices, bed-room disgust)
- **Other characters**: Labarre (innkeeper); Paulin Musebois (locksmith); Mother Gerbaud (visitor); Little Gervais (robbed child); Maubert Isabeau (baker); Gaspard Bès (bandit); Lieutenant Cravatte (bandit); Monsieur Bombarda (restaurant-keeper); Chief of Police Anglès; Gadan Corrley (fisher); Zalis Corrley (smith); Orrald Stenson (born Salcombe, called "Orrald the Younger"); Gazek Stenson (mason, born Gulhaven); Brackick family: Volia (weaver, born Dunstead), Kadrek (glazier), Kassa (glazier, born Dunby), Tatho (chandler, born Dunstead); Dumollard (orphan turned bandit, worked and stole from age five per official documents)

## Themes
- Redemptive mercy and transformative Christian charity; power of acceptance restoring dignity
- Temptation and moral struggle; theft after mercy reveals spiritual fragmentation
- Radiance of virtue confronting corruption and despair; mystical vision as transformative catalyst
- Conscience as internal battlefield; light versus darkness; Bishop as opposing principle
- Youthful innocence, gaiety, beauty amid social fragmentation; female complexity and vulnerability
- Innocence versus emancipation; motherhood and separation; abandonment and economic despair
- Transformation through hardship; beauty destroyed by labor and poverty
- Maternal love contrasted with worldly survival necessity; destiny's contingency upon small circumstances
- Narrative atmospheric repetition suggesting cyclical fate; recurring environmental details as background to human drama
- Evil's incremental progression through habituation; souls retreating toward darkness rather than advancing toward light
- Social suffering beginning at all ages; systemic exploitation of children and vulnerable; bastardry and unmarked motherhood as economic liability
